conflict_topics: Whether alcohol should be served in the flat for the housewarming
Where/how alcoholic drinks would be stored/kept during the party (fridge vs cooler in kitchen)
Guest expectations (Agent B's manager) vs housemate religious practices
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete reasons and practical proposals (e.g., cooler box, paying back for drinks); language feels natural and situationally appropriate.
Agent D provides a clear normative reason (religion) early; others respond with practical constraints (already bought drinks, manager invited).
Resolution is explicit and concrete: storage/location condition articulated and accepted.
Minimal needless repetition; turns mostly advance the problem or propose solutions.
evaluation.final_reason: Agents agreed that alcohol may be present for guests if it is kept separate and contained in the kitchen. Agent D softened from "We don't have alcohol in the house" to: "As long as it's kept separate in the kitchen, I'm okay with it." Agent A accepted this by saying: "Okay. That works for me. A cooler in the kitchen is fine." (D allowed alcohol under a containment condition; A agreed to store it in the kitchen.)
position_change_notes: Agent D: Initially stated an absolute position against alcohol in the house (Turn 6: "We don't have alcohol in the house"). Softened to accept alcohol under a containment condition (Turn 25: "As long as it's kept separate in the kitchen, I'm okay with it.").

Agent A: Initially assumed alcohol would be part of the party and emphasized purchased drinks and guest expectations (Turn 14). Later accepted the containment compromise (Turn 26: "A cooler in the kitchen is fine.").
Agent B: Emphasized guest expectations (manager invited) but accepted the compromise once Agent D confirmed willingness (Turn 24: conditional acceptance; Turn 27: confirms settlement).
Agent C: Consistently advocated for a durable cohabitation-friendly solution and did not change stance drastically, instead facilitating discussion (Turn 16, Turn 18, Turn 28).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 4 — Agent D: "Actually, yes. I'm not comfortable with us serving alcohol at the party." (Clear substantive opposition to serving alcohol appears.)
Turn 6 — Agent D: "Because I'm Muslim. We don't have alcohol in the house." (Provides religious reason; disagreement remains unresolved.)
Turn 7 — Agent B: "I already told my colleagues from work there would be drinks." (Introduces guests' expectations, increasing stakes while D maintains refusal.)

Turn 10 — Agent B: "What if we keep it in a cooler box?" / Turn 11 — Agent D: "It's not really about the fridge. I'm just not comfortable with alcohol being served in the flat." (Proposed mitigation rejected; core disagreement persists.)

Turn 12 — Agent A: "But we all agreed to have a housewarming last week. This is the first I'm hearing about this." / Turn 13 — Agent D: "I'm sorry, I didn't think to say anything." (Tension between prior agreement and D's stance; no settlement.)

Turn 14 — Agent A: "I already bought all this, and what about the guests who are expecting it?" / Turn 15 — Agent B: "I invited my manager." (Practical consequences and important guests raise the conflict to a stronger level.)

Turn 16 — Agent C: "Can we find a way that works for everyone?" / Turn 17 — Agent D: "Can we make it a party with really good food and other kinds of drinks?" (Move toward compromise; D softens but issue not settled.)

Turn 19 — Agent D: "For the drinks Agent A bought, I can pay you back... maybe Agent B, you and your manager could go for a drink somewhere nearby before or after the party?" (Offers concession but proposes sending guests away — a solution that many find unacceptable, raising new friction.)

Turn 21 — Agent A rejects D's suggestion: "That doesn't make everyone happy... Not to send guests away." / Turn 22 — Agent D: "If we use a cooler box and keep it in the kitchen... Would that work?" (A strong objection followed by a containment compromise; conflict remains unresolved at end of round.)

Turn 23 — Agent A: "But you said earlier you weren't comfortable with any alcohol... Are you sure you're okay with this now?" / Turn 24 — Agent B: "If you're really okay with that, Agent D, then yes, that works for me." (Tension reduced; awaiting D's firm acceptance.)

Turn 25 — Agent D: "As long as it's kept separate in the kitchen, I'm okay with it." / Turn 26 — Agent A: "Okay. That works for me. A cooler in the kitchen is fine." (Explicit mutual agreement: D accepts alcohol if kept separate, A agrees to that arrangement.)
Turn 27 — Agent B: "Okay, great. So that's settled then." / Turn 28 — Agent C: "Yeah, good. Glad we sorted that out." (Participants confirm the settlement; no substantive conflict remains.)

substantive_insights: Conflict is between a housemate's religious prohibition on alcohol and others' social expectations and prior commitments (bought drinks, invited manager).
Practical containment (keeping alcohol separate in the kitchen cooler) functioned as a compromise that balanced D's concern about presence in living space with A/B's desire to offer drinks.
Monetary compensation (D offering to reimburse A) was proposed but rejected as insufficient because it would require excluding or relocating guests.
Agent C played a mediating role, shifting focus to long-term cohabitation and encouraging a mutually workable solution.
